title: Automated Causal Effect Estimation through Self-Evolving AI
claim: An LLM-driven evolutionary loop turns a task specification into an estimator that beats zero-shot generation and rivals human experts.
layout: 3 panels; workflow boxes left, embedding scatter with inset center, box plots right
description: Three-panel figure. Panel a is a left-to-right workflow of rounded boxes. An input causal task box lists data structure, assumptions and metrics. A zero-shot agent box holds an LLM proposer and initial programs. An evolve box shows an LLM ensemble mutator and a MAP-Elites archive of programs, with green arrows looping back. A grey evaluation box (fail-fast, then batch evaluation) feeds scores back, and an output list sits below. Panel b is a PCA scatter of program embeddings. Colors mark benchmarks, grey points mark baselines, and an inset line plot shows fraction of final gain rising over evolution iterations. Panel c holds two stacked box-and-strip plots comparing zero-shot, evolved and human programs on RMSE (top) and interval coverage (bottom). Evolved programs show lower error and better coverage.
caption: Overview of InferenceEvolve for causal estimator discovery. a, Schematic of the workﬂow: a causal task speciﬁcation seeds a zero-shot program, which is then iteratively improved by an LLM ensemble under benchmarkbased feedback, yielding an evolutionary trace and a ﬁnal estimator. b, Principal-component view of the programs in the OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-large embedding space across evolutions. Colors denote benchmarks (gray points denote zero-shot baselines), and darker points indicate later checkpoints within each benchmark. The inset line graph (no points obscured) summarizes normalized best-so-far progress over evolution iterations. c, ACIC 2022 (Thal and Finucane, 2023) comparison against zero-shot programs and 58 human competition submissions. Top, RMSE distributions. Bottom, empirical 90% interval coverage distributions. Across the full distribution, evolved programs improve over zero-shot generation and compare favorably with human submissions.
abstract: Causal inference is central to scientific discovery, yet choosing appropriate methods remains challenging due to the complexity of statistical methodology and real-world data. Inspired by the success of artificial intelligence in accelerating scientific software, we introduce an evolutionary framework that uses large language models to discover and iteratively refine causal methods. Across benchmarks, our estimators consistently outperform established baselines: our best estimator lay on the Pareto frontier of 58 human submissions for a recent community competition. We also extend the algorithm to achieve competitive results in settings with estimated rewards. Analysis of the evolutionary trajectories shows that agents progressively discover sophisticated strategies tailored to unrevealed data-generating mechanisms. Our findings suggest that language-model-guided evolution could be used in scientific settings with partially observed rewards such as causal inference.
